newsitem.title: USA: New Mexico tribe loses another casino battle.
newsitem.headline: New Mexico tribe loses another casino battle.

text.p: A New Mexico tribe Tuesday lost a legal battle to keep its casino open as a federal appeals court issued rulings on the state's Indian gaming industry.

The 10th Circuit Court of Appeals in Denver denied a petition by the Mescalero Apache tribe asking for permission to reopen its casino pending the resolution of a long-running dispute over gambling on Indian reservations around New Mexico.
The Mescalero were forced to close their casino Sept. 24, but New Mexico's other 10 Indian gaming tribes have so far been able to stave off closure of their operations by lodging appeals.

"I think it's all unfair. If they're going to shut us down, they should shut all the other casinos down," said Cindy Valdez, a worker at the Mescalero's Inn of the Mountain God's Resort, about 120 miles southeast of Albuquerque.
The tribe has laid off around 350 workers at the resort's "Casino Apache."
Mescalero leader Wendell Chino gave no immediate response to the ruling but he has vowed to take his tribe's struggle to the U.S. Supreme Court if necessary.
In a separate decision, the Denver court threw out an attempt by federal prosecutors to close gaming operations on the Jicarilla Apache reservation in northern New Mexico.
Indian gaming in New Mexico attracted little attention until January 1995, when Gov. Gary Johnson signed gambling agreements with 14 tribes.
The tribes wasted little time in opening glitzy, 24-hour casinos up and down the highway between Santa Fe and Albuquerque and elsewhere around the state.
In July, a New Mexico federal judge declared the casinos illegal.

Nine of the tribes jointly filed a lawsuit against the decision and were granted a stay on the closures, pending appeal, while the Jicarilla and Mescalero chose to fight their legal battles separately.
The 10th Circuit Court will hear the appeals of the nine tribes Nov. 20.
